title: {{NAME}} and the Garden at the World's Edge
moral: The most beautiful places need the most careful caretakers.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a young boy with brown hair and blue eyes, wearing a soft white linen shirt with flower embroidery, pale blue trousers, and white canvas shoes — same child, same face, same exact outfit in every image.

pages.content:
The invitation was written on a petal and slid under his door at midnight.

IT SAID: COME TO THE GARDEN AT DAWN. BRING NOTHING. NEED NOTHING. JUST COME.

It was signed with two symbols: a small wing and a small spiral horn.

{{NAME}} had read enough stories to know that this was either wonderful or a trap, and that the only way to find out was to go.

pages.content:
The garden was at the end of the longest path in Whitewater Wood, behind a gate made of woven branches that parted when he touched it.

Inside: colours he didn't have names for. Flowers that hummed. Butterflies the size of his face. Light coming from no particular direction.

At the centre: a unicorn the colour of fresh snow, and on her back, sitting with the ease of someone who did this every day, a fairy wearing a crown of green light.

"You came," said the fairy. "Good. We have a problem."

pages.content:
The problem was this: the garden was sick.

Not visibly. But the fairy, whose name was Lumen, could feel it: the magical current that ran through the garden like a river had a blockage somewhere in the roots, and her magic was too small to find it, and the unicorn's magic was too large and would damage what it touched.

"What you need," said {{NAME}}, looking around carefully, "is a size in between. Human scale."

"Precisely why we called you," said Lumen.

pages.content:
He worked through the morning: on hands and knees, following Lumen's directions, checking each root junction for the blockage.

He found it at noon: a tangle of old magic, calcified into something like a knot, deep in the garden's central root system.

Lumen used her magic to loosen it. The unicorn used a single precise touch of her horn to dissolve it. {{NAME}} used his hands to clear the debris away.

The current began flowing again. The garden brightened. The humming of the flowers rose half a note.

"There it is," said Lumen, sounding deeply relieved.

pages.content:
Lumen gave him a seed as payment: small and dark and warm.

"Plant it anywhere," she said. "Anywhere you love."

The white unicorn lowered her horn and touched his forehead once, very gently, and he saw the garden for a moment as they saw it: impossibly alive, impossibly precious.

He walked home through the wood feeling the seed warm in his pocket.

In his room that night, he put it in a small pot of soil on his windowsill and watched the moon rise over the wood.

By morning, a tiny glowing stem had appeared.
